lessons.culture: Saudi banks usually work from Sunday to Thursday, since the weekend is Friday and Saturday, and you need your هويّة (ID) or your إقامة or passport to open an account. Cash is still common, so a الصرّاف (ATM) is never far away, and people thank the clerk with الله يعطيك العافية, which is answered الله يعافيك.

lessons.culture: The post office, البريد, also sells stamps and the clerk weighs your parcel at the counter to set the price. lessons.culture: In Saudi Arabia the phone is called الجوّال, and a SIM is registered in your name, so the seller asks for your ID, iqama or passport. Most people top up their balance with a recharge card or an app, and internet packages are sold by the month. Phone shops also repair screens and sell chargers and cases.

lessons.culture: In Saudi Arabia the ambulance, الإسعاف of the Red Crescent, is 997, the police are 999 and the fire service, الدفاع المدني, is 998; in the Makkah and Madinah regions the single number 911 reaches all of them. Say where you are first, because the operator needs the address before anything else, and keep the line open. In a real scare people also shout الحقوني, which means the same as ساعدوني.

lessons.culture: After an accident do not move an injured person, and keep calm. In Saudi Arabia the ambulance is 997 and traffic police 993, and for a minor accident between cars, insurers send someone from نجم (Najm) to write the accident report, which the insurance company needs before it pays. Someone who comes through safely is told الحمد لله على السلامة, answered الله يسلّمك.

exercises.tip: الحمد لله is fixed wording, the same in every dialect. The helper answers الحمد لله على السلامة, and you reply الله يسلّمك.

lessons.culture: In a mall or a crowded place, go straight to the security guard or the information desk, who can call the child's name on the loudspeaker. challenge.title: A morning of errands

a question about the post office with فين
